opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one I get a lot. Prompting is amazing. You can get surprisingly far with a frontier model and a well-written prompt. But I think of prompting as getting you to a demo, and data is what gets you to a product.

When you prompt, you're relying entirely on what the model already knows and how it happens to generalize. That works until you hit the long tail: your specific domain, your edge cases, your customers' weird inputs. Then you find yourself stuffing more and more instructions and examples into the prompt, and it gets brittle. You change one thing and something else breaks. At some point you realize you're doing data curation anyway, just badly, inside a prompt.

The other piece is that the quality of models themselves comes down to data. If you look at what's driven progress over the last few years, architecture changes have mattered, but a huge share of the gains have come from better data: better filtering, better mixtures, better synthetic data, better post-training sets. The labs know this, which is why they invest so much in it. If you want to specialize a model, whether that's fine-tuning a smaller model to be cheaper and faster or training a reasoning model for your domain, the thing that determines success is the data you put in.

And then there's evaluation, which people underrate. Even if you only ever prompt, you need a curated eval set to know whether your prompt changes actually helped. That's data curation too.

So my view is that prompting and data curation aren't competing. Prompting is a great starting point, and models are now good enough that you can use them to help *generate and curate* data. That's a lot of what excites me. But the teams that build durable, differentiated systems are the ones that treat data as a first-class engineering problem. The model is increasingly a commodity; your data and how carefully you shape it is the moat.

r001.rationale: The response says that even when using prompts, a curated evaluation set is needed to determine whether prompt changes helped.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I get a lot. The honest answer is that prompting gets you really far, really fast, and that's exactly why people stop thinking about data. You write a prompt, you get a demo, it looks amazing, and you ship it. And then you hit this wall where the thing works 80 percent of the time and you can't figure out how to get the last 20.

And what we've seen over and over is that the last 20 percent is a data problem, not a prompt problem. You can keep adding instructions to the prompt, you can keep adding few-shot examples, but at some point the model just doesn't have enough signal about what "good" looks like for your specific task. Your task has quirks. Your users phrase things in weird ways. Your domain has edge cases the model has never seen. No amount of prompt engineering teaches the model those things in a reliable way.

So the way I think about it is that prompting is how you express intent, and data is how you express the distribution. The prompt says "summarize this customer call." The data says what a good summary of a customer call actually looks like for your company, with your terminology, your length preferences, the things you care about and the things you don't. That's not something you can compress into a paragraph of instructions.

The other thing that's changed is that the economics have flipped. A couple of years ago, curating a dataset meant hiring annotators, writing guidelines, waiting weeks. Now you can use the models themselves to generate candidates, filter them, score them, find the failure modes. So the cost of good data has come way down, which actually makes it a much better investment relative to just iterating on prompts forever.

And then there's the practical stuff. If you're relying purely on a prompt against a frontier model, you're paying frontier prices and frontier latency on every call. Once you have a curated dataset that captures your task, you can distill that into a much smaller model that's faster, cheaper, and often more accurate on your narrow problem, because you've actually shown it what you want. That's a huge deal at scale.

So I'd say data curation hasn't gone away. It's just moved. It used to be the first thing you did, and now it's the thing you do once prompting has shown you where the real problems are. The prompt is the prototype. The data is the product.

r001.rationale: The response argues that curated data teaches a model the desired task behavior and supports distillation, but it does not state that evaluating prompted outputs requires curated evaluation data.

astra-6.text:
I think prompting is powerful, but it doesn’t make the underlying data less important. A lot of what you’re able to get out of a model through a prompt comes from what that model learned during training. You can guide it toward a capability, but you can’t reliably prompt your way around something it hasn’t learned well.

And when you move from a demo to a specific application, the question becomes: Does this work consistently on the kinds of inputs my users actually have? That’s a data question, too. You need representative examples to evaluate it, understand where it fails, and decide whether you need better context, fine-tuning, or a different model.

So I see prompting and data curation as complementary. Prompting gives you a really accessible way to work with the model. Curation helps make sure the information you train on, retrieve, and evaluate against is relevant and useful. More data isn’t automatically better; the right data can make a much bigger difference.

r001.rationale: The response says representative examples are needed to evaluate how the model performs on users’ inputs and identifies curated evaluation data as part of making that assessment.

sol-6.1.text:
Prompting is powerful, but it doesn’t make the underlying data problem go away. The model’s capabilities come from the data it was trained on, and the context you give it is also data. If that context is irrelevant, incomplete, or low quality, even a very good model can struggle.

So I think curation matters at both levels. When you’re training a model, you want examples that teach it the behaviors you care about. When you’re building an application, you want to select the right information and examples for the task. Prompting gives us a new way to interact with models, but choosing what they learn from and what they see is still a big part of getting them to work reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curating training examples and application context, but does not state that evaluating prompted outputs requires curated evaluation data.
